s31.title: Forum preview of the 2026 championship divisions, post 5

bet.text: Shoot several streams of fuel at once: the team predicted a ceiling of about 30 to 35 balls per second, against about 18 for a turret.

demand.text: Score from anywhere in the alliance zone and pass across the court efficiently. The team picked robustness as its difference: tied on scoring, it would outlast opponents that broke. Against championship defense it put fast, precise alignment first.

auto.text: Two full swipes of the middle, then a partial third that loads fuel for the driver. If knocked too far off its path, the robot drives to a known recovery pose and goes back to collecting instead of emptying its hopper where it cannot score. That recovery never ran in an official match.

cycle.text: The Intake pulls fuel off the ground into the hopper. The robot aligns its heading on the hub and shoots while not moving. Pulling the Intake in while shooting lifts the hopper floor, so gravity helps with the last balls.

gave_up.text: It does not shoot on the move, because of current limits and practicality. Packaging for width left about 1.25 in on either side of the feeder plates.
Shooter motors drew 100 A each at spin-up before limits, and before its Silicon Valley event the robot browned out within a minute of normal match play.
A commenter notes shot blockers were used against it on Einstein.

changed.text: The hopper floor went through four versions, the first on the Alphabot; the third still let balls under it, and the fourth, for Worlds, fixed that. Broken polycarbonate intake racks became SRPP and titanium, a second intake roller came before the third event, and a net raised capacity. Corner-centered turning was added the week before the championship.

outcome.text: 65-6-0 in official play; won the Curie division; pick 1 of the Curie alliance on Einstein; ranked 10 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 321.71, Curie).

endgame.text: No climb from the state championship on: the L3 climber the team was still trying to fit for its first event (12 lb, or 12 to 14 lb in a later post) was removed, and new bumpers dropped its cutout.

solves.text: Leave room for a continuous powered hopper floor

facts.text: Four SDS MK5n modules
The front modules were reoriented wide-ways on the competition robot so the whole hopper floor could be powered
Bumpers built for the state championship and Worlds have a smaller bottom fillet so the robot does not surf on fuel

solves.text: Pull fuel off the ground fast without breaking in collisions

cost.text: The most iterated part of the robot: polycarbonate racks broke consistently and aluminum kicker plates kept bending
The welded beater bar never broke at its tabs or welds, but the outermost 1/4 in vertical plate sometimes bent into the main roller

In hindsight the team would use a polycarbonate roller or a tube bar; a motor per side with a lower-friction slide, retracting on impact more easily, would have made the intake much lighter and simpler

facts.text: Racks are two layers of about 1/4 in SRPP and one layer of about 1/8 in titanium
A main roller of about 3 in feeds kicker bars tuned for low compression without dead spots
A second roller keeps fuel already in the hopper out of the way of fuel coming in
The rollers are dual driven by Kraken X60s
Deployment became fully gear driven mid-season, because impacts sheared timing belt teeth
The titanium is 1/8 in grade 5, cut to order in about a week; expensive, and the team calls it incredibly durable

functions.name: Hopper

solves.text: Hold fuel robustly, with fewer parts to interfere with each other

functions.type: net hopper on fixed bumper panels

facts.text: The team site says 70+ fuel; the interview says about 75 to 80 with the net, up from about 50
Panels rise from the bumpers, which adds width and cuts interference
A carbon fiber hoop adds rigidity, and carbon fiber corners replaced polycarbonate ones that cracked
Two sizes of one brand of zip ties broke on the net; another brand solved it
The net eventually replaced a solid roof

functions.name: Hopper floor

solves.text: Move fuel to the feeder with no dead spots, and empty the last balls

cost.text: The Alphabot version bound and let belts climb off pulleys; the next jammed on balls trapped underneath and fell apart in an event final when a set screw backed out
After strengthening it probably weighed about the same as roller floors; the team would maybe use another design
A team member says the tilt helps ball rate a little but is not worth the complexity, design time and tight width packaging with the intake
Belt center distance took many floor iterations: too loose and belts crawled off the pulleys, too tight and resistance was terrible

functions.type: pivoting belt floor linked to the intake

facts.text: The floor pivots with intake deploy: the intake stows under it, and retracting while shooting lifts it
On the Silicon Valley event version, evenly spaced belts were slightly better than belts grouped into four lanes; number found sufficient
Rubber-backed belts give fuel more continuity than rollers
The Worlds version has fixed belt centers, welded triangular plates, glued pulleys and a fully captured cam follower
Carbon tube rollers on the Silicon Valley event version were chosen partly for stiffness and weight; the 0.96 in outer diameter also allowed smaller 20-tooth pulleys and more hopper volume

Worlds version: a Delrin cam roller on the intake rack runs in a captured track in a 3/16 in aluminum plate on the floor, held sideways by a large washer; the last 1.5 in or so is open so the floor lifts for the battery and electronics
It pivots only enough to clear the intake roller by about 1/4 in, because of the floor's compression against the feeder rollers
The cam track was drawn in a sketch from four matched floor and intake positions, smoothed with splines
When shooting, the intake stops about 3 in short of fully stowed; fully stowed compresses the fuel too much
In a wooden prototype rollers and rubber-backed belts worked equally well, but belts could be lighter

functions.name: Feeder and drum shooter

solves.text: Bring many balls to the same speed at once, from anywhere in the zone and for passing

cost.text: Early on the shooter, free-spinning floor and feeder together browned the robot out
Load is high on the floor at first, then on the feeder; a team member thinks 2910 was right to chain both to four shared motors, despite less separable subsystems

functions.type: full-width drum shooter with adjustable hood

facts.text: Width of the shooter
Each ball touches the main drum, bottom feeder roller and top hood roller at once, so it does not wobble
A double-sided belt drives the drum on one face and the hood rollers in reverse on the other, because a pulley plus a gear did not fit
Cat tongue replaced bare polycarbonate on the feeder backing, which slipped
At the championship the team put its rate at about 25 to 28 balls per second with fresh balls
A later team post puts its rate at about 22 to 24 balls per second, typically about the same as most similar dumpers
By January 12 a kitbot upgraded with more wheels and four shooter motors had shown that a multi-ball-wide stream does not collide in the air
The Alphabot, with the same motor count and roller sizes, showed how much inertia to add and which ratios balance ball rate against current
The Alphabot exposed flexible hopper walls, feeding choke points, belt tracking problems and too little shooter inertia

functions.name: Vision

solves.text: Locate the robot well enough to aim shots and passes and run autonomous

functions.type: four AprilTag cameras on a Jetson

facts.text: Two cameras of about 120 fps on the shooter side and two of about 60 fps on the sides, all grayscale and global shutter
Custom GPU-accelerated tag detection on one Jetson Orin Nano keeps the shooter-side cameras above about
Single-tag estimates are thrown out; only multi-tag poses are used
Poses go to the robot controller by UDP, where they are filtered

cost.text: The JST connector on the Arducam OV9281 modules gave trouble, and camera wiring changed between the second event and the state championship

functions.name: Heading control

solves.text: Align quickly and precisely under defense, since the robot cannot shoot on the move

functions.type: predicted-pose heading control with a movable center of rotation

facts.text: It looks ahead to a predicted pose and adds feedforward from where the driver is moving
It can pivot about a chosen corner when in front of the tower, beside a robot or being bumped

cost.text: A commenter estimated during the championship that it spent 3 seconds in its alliance zone not shooting, against about 0.5 s for 4414

solves.text: Win the race to the middle without wasting fuel when knocked off path

facts.text: Paths are optimized ahead of time, not computed on the fly as in 2025
If the robot's pose is too far from the path, it moves to a recovery path and resumes the later stages
Choreo trajectories made the bulk of the autos, with no PathPlanner, for simple control logic and the fastest run to the neutral zone
Each swipe is a stage with around 10 variations: out through the trench, collect, then, since the state championship, back over the bump to a set shooting pose

cost.text: The recovery branch, added for the state championship after 115 blocked its trench in a Silicon Valley match, never ran in an official match, but worked quite well in one or two practice matches

Detecting a climb onto fuel from roll and pitch and backing off, tried the week before Worlds, was scrapped: the reaction was too hard to tune, and mechanical changes had made the robot much less prone to it

functions.name: Current limits and battery charge
functions.type: current limits that change with robot state

facts.text: Current limits came from log spikes, lowered by feel until the robot ran a practice session of about 3 minutes without browning out; draw was not calculated ahead
A team member calls a battery under 13.5 V on a Battery Beak risky; the beak reads high just off the charger, and the driver station later shows about 12.6 to 13 V

decisions.because: the predicted ceiling was about 30 to 35 balls per second, against about 18 for a turret with no gaps between balls
even when tied on scoring, a robot that does not break can outlast its opponents
its fibers take load around bolt holes, where polycarbonate cracked; it is lighter and more impact resistant
they give fuel more continuity than bobbling along rollers
decisions.cost: several redesigns; the team would maybe choose differently

decisions.choice: Even belt spacing across the floor
decisions.because: slow motion video and ball rate counts showed it slightly better
decisions.instead_of: belts paired into four lanes to match the shooter

decisions.choice: Continuous dead axle on the floor
decisions.because: a split axle joined by a set screw bowed, then came apart in a final
decisions.instead_of: a split shaft with a set screw, which the team urges others not to use

decisions.because: the team chose to set the tension once, with welded triangular plates adding rigidity
identifying the worst offenders by telemetry was not enough; limits on the floor, feeder and swerve change with full-field passing, corner shots, motion (which mattered little) and auto

decisions.choice: Drive intake deployment entirely by gears
decisions.because: impacts on linear intakes sheared timing belt teeth

decisions.choice: Spend the freed climber weight on a tougher intake
decisions.because: the intake came apart at the first district event, and removing a climber of about 12 to 14 lb left weight to spend

decisions.choice: Slit the rubber backing of the floor belts
decisions.because: it cut the floor's current draw around the tight bends by roughly 20 percent or more, which the team calls really important
decisions.cost: many hours of hand cutting with a printed jig: 190 slits per belt, eight belts per floor

decisions.choice: USB cameras of 1 MP at 120 FPS
decisions.because: the full rate gives lower latency and more frequent pose updates, and coax would be hard to make as reliable and easy to validate as USB
decisions.instead_of: ThriftyCams, which it evaluated, and a coax link

decisions.choice: Commit to the dumper after the Alphabot
decisions.because: the Alphabot, built by about January 20, was so good that the team stopped looking at turrets after about January 21
decisions.instead_of: maybe rebuilding to a turret later; dye rotor turrets were explored in parallel

decisions.choice: Alphabot with a fixed intake and hopper
decisions.because: a static intake and hopper made it much simpler and easy to iterate, and having no moving wiring helped wire it quickly

decisions.choice: Torque motor power screws to 1.2 N m
decisions.because: it helps keep them from backing out, and the team has seen no motor damage from it
a remedy the team lists for CANivore USB dropouts, after USB logging drives on unshielded extensions proved the cause in several robots it saw
decisions.cost: limited write cycles, so the team recommends endurance cards and fits a fresh one before each event
